articles.card: The four places that must work on day one, what can safely wait, and who actually checks the house before someone comes home.
articles.meta: What the home needs before a hospital discharge: bathroom, bed, path and entry, what can wait, and who checks it. By a Doctor of Physical Therapy.
articles.abstract: Falls are most likely in the first two weeks after a hospital stay, yet no one on the discharge team is required to walk through the house. This article gives families a short, prioritized checklist for the four places that must work on day one: the bathroom (toilet transfers, a shower chair or tub bench, properly anchored grab bars), the bed (height, lighting, a bedside commode if needed), the path between them (walker width, rugs, cords, night lighting) and the entry (railings, threshold ramps, lighting). It separates urgent changes from projects that can wait, such as walk-in showers, widened doors and stair lifts. It closes with who should check the home, citing evidence that clinician-led home hazard changes reduce falls, especially for people at higher risk.
articles.thumb: A calm, sunlit Florida bedroom and hallway seen from the bed: a walker parked beside the bed, a night light glowing low along the path to an open bathroom door, a shower chair visible inside. Optional text overlay: 'Ready for day one.' Palette: Deep Blue #0B3D62 with Sky Blue and Sun Yellow accents.
articles.alt: A walker beside a bed, with a lit path to an open bathroom door where a shower chair waits.

articles.card: Physical therapists, occupational therapists, ATPs, CAPS builders and free contractor checks compared, with six questions to ask anyone who assesses a home.
articles.meta: Who should do a home safety assessment? How PTs, OTs, ATPs, CAPS builders and contractors differ, and six questions to ask any assessor.
articles.abstract: Many people offer home safety assessments, from franchise contractors to care agencies to licensed therapists. This article explains the difference between checking a house for hazards and matching the house to the person who lives there. It compares occupational therapists, physical therapists, RESNA Assistive Technology Professionals, NAHB Certified Aging-in-Place Specialists, short-course certificate holders and contractor 'free checks' in a side-by-side table. It cites a randomized trial in which occupational therapist home assessments cut falls by nearly half while assessments by trained non-therapists had no significant effect. It explains where contractors fit and why the same company assessing and selling the fix is a conflict of interest, and it ends with six questions families should ask any assessor before booking.
articles.thumb: Split composition: on the left, a clinician kneeling beside an older adult rising from a chair with a gait belt and clipboard; on the right, a contractor's tape measure and toolbox. A subtle dividing line between them. Optional overlay: 'Who should check the house?'
articles.alt: A clinician watching an older adult stand from a chair, beside a contractor's tape measure and toolbox.

articles.card: Why one step down is riskier than a full staircase, and three ways to make a sunken living room work for a walker user.
articles.meta: How to make a sunken living room safe for a walker: railings and contrast, ramp length by step height, or changing how rooms are used.
articles.abstract: A single step down into a sunken living room is easy to miss, especially when the same flooring covers both levels. This article explains why short flights of one or two steps are overrepresented among hazardous stairs, and why a walker, which needs both hands and a level surface, makes the step harder. It lays out three options. First, add a graspable railing, a contrasting edge strip and better lighting, with therapist-taught technique. Second, replace the step with a ramp, using a table of ramp lengths for 4 to 8 inch steps at 1:12, 1:16 and 1:20 slopes. Third, move daily living to the main level. It closes with when a professional assessment is worth getting before spending money on a ramp.
articles.thumb: A 1970s-style sunken living room with one carpeted step down; a bright contrasting strip along the step edge and a new handrail beside it; a rollator paused at the top. Warm afternoon light. Optional overlay: 'One step, three solutions.'
articles.alt: A rollator at the top of a single step into a sunken living room, with a handrail and a contrasting strip on the step edge.

articles.card: Raised tracks, heavy impact glass and a step down to a wet lanai: how to check a sliding door and fix it without breaking its storm rating.
articles.meta: Is a lanai sliding door a fall risk? Track height, door weight, clear width for walkers and wheelchairs, threshold ramps, and what not to remove.
articles.abstract: Florida lanai sliders are built to keep out wind-driven rain, which often means a raised track, heavy impact-rated glass and a step down to a lanai floor that can be wet. This article walks families through four checks: track height compared with accessibility limits, how hard the door is to open and close, the real clear width of a two-panel slider compared with walkers, rollators and wheelchairs, and what waits on the other side. It then lists fixes from simplest to biggest, including threshold ramps, lighting, non-slip surfaces, a vertical grab bar and door service. It warns against removing the sill, because the sill is part of how the door resists water in a storm and changes belong to a licensed contractor.
articles.thumb: Close-up, low angle of a rollator's front wheels meeting the raised aluminum track of a sliding glass door, with a screened pool lanai and palm fronds beyond. Optional overlay: 'Mind the track.'
articles.alt: A rollator's front wheels at the raised track of a sliding glass door opening onto a screened Florida lanai.

articles.card: Utilities will not restore you first. Backup oxygen, battery planning, generator safety and Tampa Bay special needs registration, before June.
articles.meta: Keep a power wheelchair or oxygen working in a Florida hurricane: backup oxygen, batteries, generators, special needs registry and county shelters.
articles.abstract: For people who rely on oxygen, a power wheelchair or other electric medical equipment, a hurricane is a power problem first. This article explains why utility medical programs in Florida do not promise priority restoration, then gives practical guidance for oxygen (backup cylinders, run times, portable concentrator batteries, power station limits and fire safety) and for power wheelchairs (charging, manufacturer guidance, generator compatibility and a manual chair backup). It covers carbon monoxide risk from generators, how to find your evacuation zone, what the Florida Special Needs Registry does and does not do, and how special needs shelters work, with contact numbers for Hillsborough, Pinellas and Manatee counties. It urges families to write the plan in May, not September.
articles.thumb: A power wheelchair and a portable oxygen concentrator beside a charging station and a battery power station, with a window showing storm clouds and bending palms. A printed checklist on the table. Optional overlay: 'Plan in May, not September.'
articles.alt: A power wheelchair and portable oxygen concentrator charging indoors while storm clouds gather outside the window.

articles.card: Where grab bars usually go, what the standards say, how to anchor them, and why suction cups and towel bars are not the answer.
articles.meta: What grab bars do you need in the bathroom? Placement at the tub, shower and toilet, ADA dimensions, anchoring, and why a fitted plan beats a kit.
articles.abstract: The bathroom is where most home injuries among older adults happen, mostly at the tub or shower and the toilet. This article explains that most people need two to four grab bars and that placement should follow how the person moves, not a kit. A table shows typical locations and what each bar is for. The article summarizes ADA grab bar dimensions as a reference while explaining why a home should be individualized. It covers correct anchoring into studs or blocking, special care for tile and fiberglass, and why suction-cup bars, towel bars and soap dishes should never be relied on. It cites research showing grab bars help people recover their balance, notes that Original Medicare does not pay for grab bars, and describes a fitted plan.
articles.thumb: A clean, bright walk-in shower with a vertical grab bar at the entry, a horizontal bar on the back wall, a shower chair and a handheld shower head. A second small inset shows a toilet with a side-wall bar. Optional overlay: 'The right bar in the right place.'
articles.alt: A walk-in shower fitted with a vertical entry grab bar, a horizontal back-wall bar, a shower chair and a handheld shower head.

articles.card: Signs the home is still working, signs it is not, what the evidence says about making it work, and the four questions an assessment answers.
articles.meta: Can a parent age in place at home? Signs it is working, signs it is not, what the CAPABLE program shows, and what a home assessment answers.
articles.abstract: Most adults over 50 want to stay in their homes, but very few homes are built for it. This article helps families decide whether a parent can age in place by looking at three things: how the parent moves and manages daily tasks, how well the house supports that, and who can step in when needed. It lists clinician-observed signs that the arrangement is working and signs that it may not be, from repeated falls to sleeping in a recliner. It summarizes the CAPABLE program, in which an occupational therapist, a nurse and a handyman reduced difficulty with daily activities by about 30 percent. It closes with four practical questions a home safety assessment can answer so families can plan instead of react.
articles.thumb: An older father and adult daughter at a kitchen table with coffee, looking through photos of rooms on a tablet; through the doorway, a hallway with a new grab bar and good lighting. Warm, hopeful tone. Optional overlay: 'Stay, adapt, or plan a move?'
articles.alt: An older man and his adult daughter reviewing photos of the home on a tablet at the kitchen table.

articles.card: The planning call, the 60 to 120 minute visit, the fall risk tests we use, and the written photo report and prioritized plan you keep.
articles.meta: What happens during a home safety visit: the planning call, what to have ready, STEADI fall risk tests, the room-by-room walkthrough and your report.
articles.abstract: Families often hesitate to book a home safety visit because they do not know what to expect. This article walks through all three parts. Before the visit, a 30-minute Initial Consultation plans the visit, and a checklist explains what to have ready, from medication lists to the shoes the person usually wears. During the visit, the clinician assesses the person with CDC STEADI screening tools, explained in a table with their risk thresholds, then walks the home room by room using structured assessment methods. After the visit, the family receives a photo report, a prioritized hazard list and specific recommendations, with an optional contractor-ready prescription. It also explains how health information is protected and shared.
articles.thumb: A clinician with a tablet and measuring tape standing in a hallway with an older woman using a cane, both looking toward the bathroom; a numbered photo report layout floats subtly in the corner. Optional overlay: 'What to expect.'
articles.alt: A clinician with a tablet and tape measure walking through a hallway with an older woman who uses a cane.

articles.card: Why free safety checks are usually sales appointments, what a clinician sees that a contractor may not, and your rights when you sign at home.
articles.meta: Is a free contractor home safety check really free? The sales incentive, what a clinician adds, Florida cancellation rights, and how to hire safely.
articles.abstract: Free in-home safety checks from companies that sell stair lifts, walk-in tubs and installation work are usually lead generation. This article explains the incentives without condemning contractors: the fix tends to match the product line, the person is not assessed, and pressure to sign today is a sales tactic. It cites trial evidence on the value of clinician-led assessment and lists what a licensed clinician looks for that a contractor may not. A table summarizes consumer protections, including the FTC Cooling-Off Rule, Florida's home solicitation cancellation rights, Florida's contractor deposit rule and added penalties for deceptive practices against older adults. It closes with five steps before hiring anyone and the practice's independence policy.
articles.thumb: A friendly salesperson with a branded clipboard and a glossy brochure at a front door, while an older homeowner holds a pen over a contract; a small magnifying glass icon over the fine print. Keep it light, not sinister. Optional overlay: 'Free for whom?'
articles.alt: A salesperson with a clipboard at a front door while an older homeowner considers a contract.

articles.card: Make video calls a real safety check, choose technology your parent agrees to, and build a local team you can call within an hour.
articles.meta: How to check on a parent's safety from another state: video walkthroughs, sensors and alerts, privacy, and a local team with Tampa Bay contacts.
articles.abstract: More than one in ten family caregivers live an hour or more from the person they care for. This article gives long-distance families a three-part approach. First, turn monthly video calls into a structured safety walkthrough, with what to look for in the kitchen, bathroom, walking paths, mail and medications, and in the parent. Second, choose technology with the parent rather than for them, using a table comparing medical alert buttons, automatic fall detection, motion and door sensors, smart speakers and medication dispensers, and their limits, including privacy. Third, build a local team that can be at the house within an hour, with national and Tampa Bay aging-network phone numbers and a pointer to geriatric care managers.
articles.thumb: A split scene: an adult child on a laptop video call in a northern city apartment at dusk; on the screen, a parent in a bright Florida living room holding a phone up to show a hallway. A faint dotted line connects the two. Optional overlay: 'Close, from far away.'
articles.alt: An adult child on a video call with a parent in Florida who is showing a hallway on the phone camera.

articles.card: Threshold ramps, full ramps, platform lifts and stair lifts compared on rise, space and cost, plus pre-built ramp options and how to choose.
articles.meta: Ramp, threshold ramp or lift? Slope rules, ramp length by rise, space, cost ranges, pre-built and rental ramps, and which fits your home.
articles.abstract: Families often ask for 'a ramp' when the real need could be a small threshold ramp, a full ramp or a lift. This article compares all four options on the rise they handle, the space they need, typical costs and whether they need power. It explains the 1:12 slope rule, gives ramp lengths for common rises at 1:12, 1:16 and 1:20, and explains why gentler slopes suit more people. It covers landings, width, handrails and edge protection, then compares pre-built options: threshold ramps, portable folding ramps, residential and commercial modular aluminum systems, and rental with installation, using listed manufacturer and retailer prices. It notes that Original Medicare does not pay for ramps or stair lifts.
articles.thumb: Three simple side-by-side illustrations on a light background: a small threshold ramp at a door, a modular aluminum ramp with handrails up to a porch, and a vertical platform lift beside entry steps. Brand colors, clean line style. Optional overlay: 'Which one fits?'
articles.alt: Illustrations of a threshold ramp, a modular aluminum ramp to a porch, and a vertical platform lift beside entry steps.

articles.card: Most night falls happen on the way to the bathroom. Light the path, set up the bed, get up in stages, and review medicines with the prescriber.
articles.meta: How to prevent falls at night: automatic lighting, bed height and bedside setup, a clear route to the bathroom, getting up slowly, and medication review.
articles.abstract: Night falls stack several risks at once: grogginess, darkness, a drop in blood pressure on standing, urgency to reach the toilet and bedtime medications. This article summarizes the evidence linking night-time urination, orthostatic hypotension and fall-risk medications to falls. It then gives five practical steps: light the path automatically with motion-sensor and low night lighting, set up the bed and bedside, clear and shorten the route to the bathroom, teach a slow get-up routine, and ask the prescriber or pharmacist to review sleep aids, water pills and blood pressure medicines. It points to the CDC's STEADI-Rx program for pharmacist medication review and explains when a home visit can map and fix the exact night route.
articles.thumb: A dark bedroom at night with a soft amber motion-sensor light strip along the floor leading from the bed to a partly open bathroom door; slippers by the bed. Deep blue night tones with warm amber light. Optional overlay: 'Light the way.'
articles.alt: A dark bedroom with a soft amber floor light guiding the way from the bed to the bathroom door.

articles.card: One story is a start, not the finish. Florida-specific traps, a ten-point tour checklist, and how to buy for the next 20 years.
articles.meta: Should you buy a one-story home before retiring in Florida? Accessibility data, flood elevation, sliders and garage steps, and a 10-point tour checklist.
articles.abstract: A one-story home is a good start for retirement, but it is not the same as an accessible home. Harvard housing research shows fewer than 4 percent of U.S. homes combine a no-step entry, single-floor living and doors wide enough for a wheelchair. This article explains Florida-specific traps: flood-elevation rules that put steps at every door, tall sills on hurricane-rated sliders, garage steps without railings, pools and lanais, and sunken rooms. It gives buyers a ten-point tour checklist covering entries, doors, hallways, bathroom, bedroom, kitchen, thresholds, laundry, lighting and storm plans, and uses the visitability standard as a minimum. It encourages buying for the next 20 years and describes a pre-purchase assessment.
articles.thumb: A buyer couple in their 60s on a home tour in a Florida ranch house, one holding a tape measure across a doorway, the other looking at a front entry with two steps; a real estate sign and palm tree visible outside. Optional overlay: 'Buy for the next 20 years.'
articles.alt: A couple on a home tour measuring a doorway in a one-story Florida house.

articles.card: What Medicare may and may not cover, other programs that can help, and how our home safety consultations are paid.
articles.meta: Does Medicare pay for a home safety assessment? When Medicare may cover part of it, what it does not cover, and other programs that can help.
articles.abstract: Families often assume Medicare pays for a home safety assessment and the grab bars that follow. This article explains that Original Medicare does not list an independent home safety assessment as a covered benefit and does not pay for grab bars, ramps or stair lifts. A table explains when Medicare may cover related care: home health therapy for homebound patients, outpatient physical or occupational therapy under a plan of care, and the fall risk review in the Annual Wellness Visit. It then covers other programs that may help: Medicare Advantage supplemental benefits, Florida Medicaid long-term care home accessibility adaptations, VA HISA grants and medical expense tax rules. It closes with how the practice's consultations are paid, without listing prices.
articles.thumb: A kitchen table with a Medicare card (generic, no real numbers), a calculator, a folded grab bar brochure and a notepad with a question mark; soft morning light. Optional overlay: 'Who pays?'
articles.alt: A generic Medicare card, a calculator and a notepad with a question mark on a kitchen table.

articles.card: Independence is a fit between a person and a place. Five areas of the home that keep a parent going out, moving, and cooking for themselves.
articles.meta: Help an aging parent stay independent at home: easy exits, fixes fitted to how they move, room to stay active, a reachable kitchen and a driving plan.
articles.abstract: Independence depends on the home as much as the person. This article covers five areas: getting out the door (garage steps, heavy doors, slider tracks, dark walkways), fitting changes such as grab bars to how a parent actually moves, setting the house up to encourage daily movement, keeping the kitchen within safe reach, and planning for the car transfer and for the day driving stops. It cites CDC data that more than one in four adults 65 and older falls each year.
articles.thumb: An older woman in her late 70s confidently stepping out of a bright Florida front door onto a well-lit walkway, one hand lightly on a new sturdy handrail, a tote bag on her shoulder, palm and sunny sky beyond. No text. Palette: Deep Blue #0B3D62 with Sky Blue #5B9BD5 and Sun Yellow #F4B400 accents.
articles.alt: An older woman stepping out her front door, one hand on a sturdy handrail, on her way out for the day.

articles.card: Why staying home is worth it, the Florida ranch-home traps that get in the way, and four signs aging in place can work.
articles.meta: The benefits of aging in place in Tampa Bay, the Florida home features that make it harder, and four signs it can work for you or a parent.
articles.abstract: Most older adults want to stay home; AARP found 75 percent of adults 50 and older want to remain in their current home. This article explains the benefits (control over daily life, familiarity, neighbors and community in places like Sun City Center, Apollo Beach and Brandon), then the common Florida ranch-home traps: sunken rooms and garage steps, raised slider tracks, slick tile, garden tubs, narrow bathrooms and no storm plan for powered medical equipment. It gives four signs aging in place may work and explains how a Home Safety Visit or Right Home Assessment helps.
articles.thumb: A single-story Florida ranch home at golden hour, seen from the front walk: a tidy entry, a screened lanai to one side, a neighbor waving from the next driveway. Warm, welcoming, slightly aspirational. No text. Palette: Deep Blue #0B3D62 with Sky Blue #5B9BD5 and Sun Yellow #F4B400 accents.
articles.alt: A single-story Florida ranch home at golden hour with a neighbor waving from the next driveway.

articles.card: Hazard hunts, night light patrol, tech help and storm prep: age-by-age safety jobs grandkids can take on, and what to leave to adults.
articles.meta: Age-by-age home safety jobs for grandkids: hazard hunts, night lights, tech setup, moving items within reach, storm prep, and what to leave to adults.
articles.abstract: Family caregivers raising children can share some of the load. This article gives age-by-age home safety jobs for grandchildren: a hazard hunt for rugs, cords and clutter (5 and up), night light patrol along the bed-to-bathroom route (7 and up), tech help with smart speakers, favorites, video calls and reminders (10 and up), moving everyday items within safe reach (10 and up), storm prep for teens, and noticing changes in how a grandparent moves. It is clear that kids should not help with standing, walking, transfers or bathing.
articles.thumb: A 10-year-old grandchild kneeling in a sunny Florida hallway, pressing a motion-sensor night light into a wall outlet near the floor, while the grandfather stands beside them smiling; a small handwritten checklist on a clipboard beside them. No text. Palette: Deep Blue #0B3D62 with Sky Blue #5B9BD5 and Sun Yellow #F4B400 accents.
articles.alt: A grandfather and grandchild plugging a motion-sensor night light into a hallway outlet together.
